paper_did: Synthesized an interstitial high‐entropy alloy (iHEA) with a nominal composition Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 using vacuum induction melting, hot‐rolling, homogenization, quenching, and further grain refinement by cold‐rolling and short annealing.

Employed extensive microstructural characterizations (XRD, EBSD, EDS, TEM, APT) to assess the dual‐phase microstructure (f.c.c. matrix and h.c.p. phase) and the distribution of interstitial carbon and nano‐sized carbide precipitates.
Conducted tensile tests at room temperature on both coarse‐grained and grain‐refined samples to evaluate yield strength, ultimate strength, ductility, and strain‐hardening behavior.
paper_reported: Identified that the iHEA exhibits a dual‐phase microstructure where the metastable f.c.c. matrix undergoes strain‐induced martensitic (TRIP) transformation and develops nano‐twinning (TWIP) during deformation, both contributing to enhanced strain hardening.
Documented that intragranular nano‐carbides (M23C6 type) are uniformly distributed in the refined microstructure and provide additional strengthening via an Orowan mechanism.

Demonstrated that the combined effect of interstitial and substitutional solid solution strengthening, phase transformation, nano‐twinning, and grain size reduction results in an exceptional balance of strength and ductility.
paper_proposed: Highlighted the broad optimization potential of using interstitial alloying to tune phase stability and deformation mechanisms.
Suggested that further refinement of processing parameters and microstructural tailoring could further enhance the strength–ductility combination and pave the way for commercial application.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Long-term exposure to elevated service temperatures induces coarsening of precipitates in the HEA, leading to a brittle intermetallic network that embrittles the matrix by depleting ductility‐enhancing elements.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy originally designed as a single-phase solid solution with a homogeneous distribution of constituent elements.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject specimens to prolonged thermal aging at service-relevant elevated temperatures (e.g., 900 °C for extended durations) to intentionally drive precipitate coarsening.
hypotheses.conditions: Aging in air or inert atmosphere at ~900 °C for times significantly longer than the initial annealing step in the paper, followed by mechanical loading at room temperature and moderate to high stress levels typical of demanding engineering service.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Coarse intermetallic precipitates (e.g., Ni3Ti-like phases) that form a continuous network or clusters at grain boundaries, accompanied by a local depletion of ductility-promoting elements from the matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: In the paper, fine Ni3Ti precipitates generated via friction stir alloying and controlled annealing created local Ni-depletion that activated beneficial TRIP in a refined microstructure (PMC7810985::web::009::fsa_and_fsa_anneal and PMC7810985::web::012::fsa_and_fsa_anneal). However, during long-term aging, these precipitates can coarsen. The larger, more continuous intermetallic phases act as stress concentrators and weak links at grain boundaries, impeding effective dislocation motion and deformation twin nucleation. This transforms a tough, deformable matrix into one susceptible to brittle fracture under mechanical loading.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Aged specimens will show a marked reduction in toughness, with fracture surfaces displaying features of brittle intergranular or quasi-cleavage fracture; the yield and ultimate strengths may show less ductility compared to the as-cast single-phase baseline. The degradation may be on the order of a 30–50% reduction in toughness, although the precise value is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: HEA in the as-cast or optimally annealed condition showing a single-phase microstructure with fine precipitates that facilitate TRIP and TWIP mechanisms (PMC7810985::web::004::benchmark_from_fsp, PMC7810985::web::010::fsa_and_fsa_anneal).
hypotheses.boundary: Service operating temperatures near 900 °C and mechanical loading regimes that allow sufficient time for thermal diffusion effects; the phenomenon may not appear under short-term or low-temperature service conditions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of precipitate coarsening and the corresponding critical sizes that trigger embrittlement in this HEA system are not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens: one retained as the single-phase baseline and one subjected to long-term annealing at 900 °C for an extended period (e.g., 100 hours). Conduct identical tensile tests and fracture toughness measurements on both sets.
measurements: Fracture surface analysis (SEM/EBSD) for precipitate size and distribution
Tensile stress-strain curves and toughness (area under curve)
Quantitative phase analysis of precipitates (TEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged specimens do not exhibit significant coarsening of precipitates and maintain toughness comparable to the baseline, then the hypothesis that thermal aging causes brittle fracture via precipitate coarsening is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper's demonstration that controlled annealing leads to a deliberate Ni depletion and activation of TRIP (PMC7810985::web::012::fsa_and_fsa_anneal); here, the mechanism is extended to long-term service where excessive precipitate growth reverses the benefit.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis investigates the effect of over-aging and precipitate coarsening under long-term service conditions, which was not explored in the paper that used short-term controlled annealing to enhance properties.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Exposure to high strain rate loading at cryogenic temperatures suppresses the activation of TWIP and TRIP mechanisms in the single-phase HEA, leading to a transition toward brittle fracture.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a fine, metastable, single-phase microstructure that under ambient conditions activates TWIP and/or TRIP for ductility.
hypotheses.intervention: Process a batch of samples using an over-annealing treatment that coarsens the grain structure slightly (or omit subsequent grain refinement steps) and then subject them to high strain rate tensile tests at cryogenic temperatures.
hypotheses.conditions: Mechanical loading at high strain rates (e.g., impact or dynamic tensile test conditions) combined with cryogenic test temperatures (e.g., below 77 K) where the mobility of dislocations and twin boundaries is reduced.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Reduced density of deformation twins and inhibited martensitic transformation (or TRIP) mechanisms, coupled with potentially larger grain sizes that limit strain accommodation.
hypotheses.mechanism: The paper shows that under room temperature conditions, fine-grained HEAs processed by friction stir techniques enable TWIP and TRIP, which absorb deformation (PMC7810985::web::003::introduction and PMC7810985::web::010::fsa_and_fsa_anneal). At cryogenic temperatures and high strain rates, the energy available for dislocation motion and twin formation is lower. This suppression of the adaptive deformation mechanisms forces the material to deform by limited dislocation glide, resulting in stress concentrations and premature crack initiation leading to brittle fracture.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to a fine-grained, room temperature baseline, the cryogenic and high strain rate specimens will exhibit a sharp decrease in toughness, with stress-strain curves showing little work hardening and evidence of brittle fracture features. The drop in toughness might be significant, but the exact magnitude is uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: HEA specimens tested under conventional room temperature and quasi-static loading conditions where TWIP and TRIP are active and provide ductile behavior.
hypotheses.boundary: The phenomenon is expected under extreme conditions (very low temperatures and high strain rates) and may not be observed at moderate temperatures or strain rates.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The interplay between grain size, deformation mechanism activation, and cryogenic effects is complex; quantification of the threshold conditions for brittle behavior requires further study.

Test both sets at room temperature and cryogenic temperature under both quasi-static and high strain rate conditions. Compare the deformation response and fracture surfaces.

Fractography (SEM/EBSD) to identify deformation mode

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens at cryogenic temperatures and high strain rates still activate TWIP/TRIP mechanisms (evidenced by significant twin density or phase transformation) and do not show an abrupt drop in toughness compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s evidence that deformation mechanisms (TWIP/TRIP) contribute to toughness in HEAs (PMC7810985::web::003::introduction, PMC7810985::web::010::fsa_and_fsa_anneal), extending the investigation to extreme loading and temperature conditions where those mechanisms might be suppressed.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis explores the effect of low temperatures and high strain rate conditions on an HEA that is designed to be ductile under standard conditions, highlighting the potential for a brittle transition when the deformation mechanisms are inhibited.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Coupling mechanical loading with an aggressive, corrosive service environment induces localized chemical segregation at grain boundaries in the HEA, promoting intergranular brittle fracture.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy engineered as a single-phase solid solution with homogeneous elemental distribution and an intact passive surface layer.
hypotheses.intervention: Expose specimens to cyclic mechanical loading in a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., a chloride-containing aqueous solution) while comparing with mechanically loaded specimens in an inert (non-corrosive) environment.
hypotheses.conditions: Service conditions representative of aggressive environments (e.g., marine or industrial settings) where corrosion agents (like Cl− ions) are present, combined with cyclic (fatigue) mechanical loading at ambient to slightly elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Environmentally induced segregation and oxidation at grain boundaries, which may lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic or oxide films that compromise grain boundary cohesion.
hypotheses.mechanism: While the paper focused on controlled microstructural tuning via friction stir alloying and annealing (PMC7810985::web::012::fsa_and_fsa_anneal), this hypothesis posits that when the HEA is simultaneously subjected to mechanical fatigue and aggressive corrosion, the passive oxide layer may locally break down. This breakdown can induce elemental segregation (for instance, depletion of Ni or enrichment of other elements at grain boundaries) and facilitate the formation of brittle phases or oxides. As a result, intergranular fracture is promoted under mechanical loading, leading to a loss in overall toughness.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Specimens in the corrosive environment under cyclic loading will show lower fracture toughness, intergranular crack propagation, and more brittle fracture characteristics compared to identical specimens tested in an inert environment. The relative drop in toughness is expected to be significant, though the exact magnitude is not precisely predictable.
hypotheses.baseline: HEA specimens loaded cyclically in an inert environment, retaining homogeneous microstructure and demonstrating ductile, fatigue-resistant behavior.
hypotheses.boundary: This behavior is anticipated primarily in service conditions where both mechanical fatigue and corrosion are present; under purely mechanical or inert conditions the HEA is expected to maintain its ductile characteristics.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The degree to which corrosion accelerates segregation and brittle phase formation in HEAs under cyclic load is not fully quantified and may depend on the specific corrosive medium and loading frequency.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens with identical surface finish. Expose one set to cyclic mechanical loading in a chloride-containing aqueous environment and the other set to the same mechanical loading in an inert atmosphere (e.g., dry nitrogen). Use similar loading amplitudes and cycles. After testing, analyze fracture surfaces and perform microchemical mapping at grain boundaries.
measurements: Fracture toughness and fatigue life measurements
SEM/EDS analysis of grain boundary chemistry and oxide formation
Comparison of crack initiation sites and propagation paths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the specimens in the corrosive environment do not show any significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, brittle intergranular fracture, or a notable decrease in toughness relative to the inert control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s findings on local compositional changes altering deformation mechanisms (e.g., Ni depletion near precipitates in PMC7810985::web::012::fsa_and_fsa_anneal) are leveraged to propose that similar local compositional segregation can occur due to environmentally induced corrosion, impacting toughness.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the combined effect of mechanical fatigue and corrosive environmental attack on the HEA, an aspect not addressed in the paper, to explain potential loss of toughness through intergranular embrittlement.

paper_did: Processed an as‐cast Ni–Si5 HEA (Fe42.8Mn28.3Cr14.8Ni9.6Si4.5 at.%) using friction stir processing (FSP) and friction stir alloying (FSA) with Ti addition via pre‐drilled holes.
Optimized FSA parameters (reducing tool rotation from 600 to 150 RPM) to enable non‐equilibrium dissolution of Ti without constitutional liquation.
Applied a subsequent annealing treatment at 900 °C for 4 h to precipitate Ni3Ti, which locally depleted Ni and activated both TWIP and TRIP deformation mechanisms.
paper_reported: FSP led to dramatic grain refinement and improvements in yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility relative to the as‐cast condition, with deformation primarily via TWIP.

FSA followed by annealing produced fine Ni3Ti precipitates that create local regions of reduced Ni concentration, lowering the stacking fault energy to trigger approximately 21% deformation-induced γ → ε transformation (TRIP) alongside TWIP.

The work hardening behavior and overall mechanical response were correlated with the engineered microstructure and predicted SFE, establishing a novel microstructural architecture that combines precipitation hardening with active deformation mechanisms.
paper_proposed: Introduced a new pathway for alloy design based on local compositional tuning via friction stir alloying, suggesting that combining multiple strengthening/deformation mechanisms (PH, TWIP, TRIP) can overcome the traditional strength–ductility trade‐off.
Implied potential for further parameter optimization and application of friction-stir-based processing for modifying HEA microstructures beyond conventional casting and thermomechanical treatments.

paper_did: Utilized friction stir alloying (FSA) on as‐cast Ni–Si5–HEA by adding Ti powder into pre‐drilled holes, using optimized processing conditions (e.g., reduced tool rotation rate of 150 RPM) to ensure dissolution of Ti without causing constitutional liquation.
Performed a two‐pass FSA and then annealed the processed specimens at 900 °C for 4 hours so that Ni3Ti precipitates could form, thereby inducing a local Ni depletion in the matrix.

Characterized microstructure and mechanical properties via techniques such as EBSD, TEM, and EDS, and demonstrated that the controlled formation of Ni3Ti precipitates lowered the stacking fault energy (SFE) locally to activate a combined TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) and TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) deformation mode along with precipitate hardening.
paper_reported: A transformation from a coarse-grained as-cast state (~13.7 µm) to a refined microstructure (down to ~1.2 µm in the FSA condition) with enhanced yield and tensile strengths was achieved.

Annealing triggered the precipitation of Ni3Ti, which locally depleted Ni in the matrix and reduced SFE—corroborated by ~21% transformation from the FCC (γ) phase to the HCP (ε) phase during deformation—thus activating a mixed TWIP + TRIP mode.

The work hardening behavior of the processed specimens was successfully modeled through a strength model correlated with SFE, linking the microstructural architecture to the observed mechanical performance.
paper_proposed: A novel microstructural design strategy that uses local composition tailoring via friction stir alloying to simultaneously introduce precipitate hardening and activate multiple deformation mechanisms (TWIP and TRIP) to overcome the strength–ductility trade‐off.

The potential of scaling up FSA (or employing emerging friction-based manufacturing techniques) as a solid-state alloy modification route for designing high-performance high-entropy alloys was highlighted.

paper_did: Developed a novel friction stir alloying (FSA) process on a Ni–Si5 high‐entropy alloy (Fe42.8Mn28.3Cr14.8Ni9.6Si4.5 at.%) by pre‐placing Ti powders in drilled holes and processing with optimized parameters (e.g., reduced tool rotation rate to 150 RPM) to avoid constitutional liquation.
Implemented a two‐pass FSA process followed by an annealing treatment at 900 °C for 4 hours to promote the precipitation of fine, coherent Ni3Ti intermetallic particles within the FCC matrix.

Characterized the microstructure (via EBSD, TEM, EDS) and mechanical response (tensile testing, work hardening behavior) to demonstrate that the process yielded grain refinement and a locally tuned deformation mechanism (combined TWIP/TRIP) via Ni depletion.
paper_reported: That FSA combined with a post‐annealing treatment leads to the formation of coherent Ni3Ti precipitates, which create Ni‐depleted regions that lower local stacking fault energy and enable the activation of transformation‐induced plasticity (TRIP) in addition to the intrinsic twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP).

Substantial improvements in yield strength, tensile strength, and ductility were achieved in the FSA + Anneal condition relative to as‐cast and FSP specimens, with experimental evidence (e.g., TEM and EBSD observations) linking microstructural refinement and phase transformation behavior to enhanced mechanical properties.

Processing parameter optimization (tool rotation, heat input) was correlated with microstructural evolution and mechanical property outcomes, establishing the viability of FSA as a method for localized alloying without bulk melting.
paper_proposed: The use of friction stir alloying as a versatile, localized solid‐state alloying method to simultaneously activate multiple strengthening and deformation mechanisms (i.e., TWIP, TRIP, and precipitate hardening) in high‐entropy alloys.

Future explorations of process–structure–property relationships in HEAs through FSA, potentially tuning local compositions and microstructures to achieve enhanced engineering properties across different service regimes.

hypotheses.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy (HEA), a controlled thermal aging treatment that induces nanoscale brittle precipitates (similar in nature to the B2 phase) will reduce toughness and promote brittle fracture under mechanical loading. This occurs because these precipitates act as stress concentration sites and dislocation barriers, thereby localizing strain and facilitating crack initiation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A single-phase HEA (e.g., a CoNiV-based alloy) with a uniform solid solution microstructure.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a controlled thermal aging treatment at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 600–700 °C for a defined period) to nucleate dispersed nanoscale precipitates within the matrix.
hypotheses.conditions: Compare samples subjected to the aging treatment with untreated as-cast samples under room-temperature tensile/compression tests at moderate-to-high strains, representative of demanding service conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Nanoscale precipitates distributed within the original single-phase matrix, forming coherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
hypotheses.mechanism: The precipitates serve as effective dislocation obstacles and localize strain due to their higher intrinsic brittleness. Their interfaces with the ductile matrix concentrate stress (similar to the fcc–B2 interfacial effects observed in the paper, PMC8378815::web::011) and reduce the ability of dislocations to transfer strain uniformly, resulting in a lowered toughness and an increased likelihood of brittle fracture.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Aged HEA samples will show higher yield strength but a significant reduction in toughness (evidenced by lower fracture strain and more brittle, cleavage-type fracture surfaces) compared to the unaged control.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-cast single-phase HEA, which exhibits ductile behavior with significant plastic deformation before failure.
hypotheses.boundary: Service conditions near room temperature where loadings approach the critical stress levels and where thermal exposure similar to the aging treatment might occur inadvertently.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of toughness reduction is sensitive to precipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution; these parameters require further optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same HEA—one kept in the as-cast state and another subjected to the specified thermal aging. Conduct identical tensile tests at room temperature and perform detailed fractography (SEM/TEM) to assess fracture modes.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally aged sample does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in toughness or if fracture surfaces remain ductile (without clear cleavage or interfacial decohesion), the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies the precipitation mechanism, previously demonstrated in a dual-phase HEA, to an originally single-phase HEA via controlled thermal aging to explicitly test the loss in toughness due to induced nanoscale brittle precipitates.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Alloying a single-phase HEA with a minor amount of grain-boundary active elements (e.g., Ti or Hf) that preferentially segregate to grain boundaries will cause intergranular embrittlement under mechanical loading, leading to a transition from ductile to brittle fracture in demanding service conditions.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A single-phase HEA with a uniform distribution of principal elements and clean grain boundaries.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a small concentration (e.g., 1–2 at%) of a segregating element known to lower grain boundary cohesion into the HEA during melting.
hypotheses.conditions: Perform comparative mechanical tests (e.g., slow strain rate tensile tests) at lower temperatures where ductile-to-brittle transition is more likely, ensuring that any segregation effects become critical under service-like loading conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries enriched with the segregating element, which decrease the cohesive strength at the interfaces.
hypotheses.mechanism: The added element segregates to the grain boundaries during solidification or subsequent heat treatments, reducing local cohesion. This weakened interface facilitates intergranular crack initiation and propagation under mechanical load, thereby reducing overall toughness. This aligns with broader ductile–brittle transition principles (TXT::wikipedia::Ductility::008).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: HEA samples with the minor addition will exhibit a pronounced shift toward intergranular brittle fracture (e.g., along grain boundaries with little plastic deformation) compared to the plain HEA, which should maintain ductile failure modes under similar conditions.
hypotheses.baseline: The original single-phase HEA without additional segregating elements, displaying homogeneous plastic deformation and ductile fracture.
hypotheses.boundary: Low-temperature service conditions and slow strain rate loading where grain boundary embrittlement effects are amplified.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The degree of embrittlement depends on the solute’s segregation tendency and the resulting concentration at the grain boundaries, which may vary with processing.

hypotheses.builds_on: The general understanding from ductile–brittle transition literature (TXT::wikipedia::Ductility::008) that reduced grain boundary cohesion leads to brittle fracture, extended here to a single-phase HEA.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis explores the role of controlled grain boundary segregation in altering fracture behavior in a nominally single-phase HEA—a factor not addressed in the original paper, which focused on precipitate-induced mechanisms.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Under high strain-rate mechanical loading, a single-phase HEA lacking microstructural features that promote dynamic twin formation will exhibit brittle fracture due to insufficient strain hardening, as dislocation motion is too uniform and fails to generate the beneficial obstacles (e.g., twins) that delay crack propagation.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A single-phase HEA with a high stacking fault energy where dislocation slip dominates, and twinning mechanisms are not readily activated under standard conditions.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject the HEA to mechanical tests at varying strain rates (comparing low strain rate to high strain rate loading), without altering its composition or thermal history.
hypotheses.conditions: Mechanical testing at room temperature across a range of strain rates—from conventional (e.g., 10^−3 s^−1) to high (e.g., using a split Hopkinson pressure bar) representative of impact or high-rate service conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The density (or absence) of deformation twins that normally act to subdivide grains and impede crack propagation.
hypotheses.mechanism: At low strain rates, even in a single-phase HEA, enough time is available for some twinning to occur during plastic deformation, thereby enhancing strain hardening and toughness. However, at high strain rates, the activation time for dislocation-twin interactions is limited, and the material deforms primarily via homogeneous dislocation slip. This lack of dynamic twin formation limits the strain hardening capacity and leads to premature crack initiation and brittle fracture. This concept builds on the paper’s emphasis on twin-mediated plasticity (PMC8378815::web::012, PMC8378815::web::013).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: High strain-rate tests are expected to show lower ductility, reduced strain hardening rates, and a fracture surface indicative of brittle failure (e.g., cleavage facets) compared to low strain-rate tests where ductile features (e.g., dimples and twins) are present.
hypotheses.baseline: The performance of the single-phase HEA under low strain-rate loading, where ductile fracture dominated by twinning and dislocation slip is observed.
hypotheses.boundary: Service applications involving high strain-rate loading, such as impact or crash scenarios, where typical strain rates exceed those used in standard quasi-static tests.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The threshold strain rate at which the transition from ductile to brittle behavior occurs is not precisely known and might depend on subtle microstructural features.

paper_did: Developed a dual‐phase (fcc + B2) CoNiV‐based alloy by minor Al addition (Al5(CoNiV)95 and Al7(CoNiV)93) using arc-melting, suction‐casting, cold rolling, and annealing.
Processed the alloys to obtain controlled precipitation of Al‐rich B2 nanoparticles dispersed in a predominantly fcc matrix.
Characterized the microstructure and phase composition via XRD, EBSD, TEM, and EDS, and quantified the volume fractions and grain sizes of the fcc and B2 phases.

Tested tensile properties over a wide temperature range (77 K, 298 K, 723 K, and 1073 K) and analyzed the deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning, stacking faults, dynamic strain aging, dynamic recrystallization) contributing to the ultrahigh strength‐ductility synergy
paper_reported: Achieved ultrahigh tensile yield strengths (e.g., ~1.1 GPa at room temperature and higher at cryogenic conditions) combined with excellent ductility (up to ~34% at 298 K and superplastic behavior at 1073 K).

Identified multiple strengthening and toughening mechanisms such as precipitation strengthening, grain boundary strengthening, twin‐mediated plasticity (with dynamic Hall‐Petch effects), and dynamic strain aging that contribute to the superior mechanical performance.

Observed that B2 nanoprecipitates not only add to yield strength via precipitation hardening but also act as stress concentrators which, when locally mitigated by twin formation, help delay crack initiation.
paper_proposed: Explored a compositional tuning strategy (i.e., increasing Al content from 5 to 7 at%) to adjust the volume fraction of the B2 phase, thereby offering an additional pathway to optimize the strength–ductility balance over a wide temperature range.
Suggested that the precipitation‐strengthening concept, coupled with conventional mechanisms, could be further adapted to design lightweight, high‐performance M/HEAs.

expert_context.question: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Brittleness in the HEA emerges when enhanced grain-boundary segregation (via a minor addition of Zr) disrupts the phase boundary-mediated dislocation transfer.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A single-phase, compositionally complex HEA with an enamel-like, dual-phase nanolamellar structure exhibiting stabilized FCC/BCC phase boundaries.
hypotheses.intervention: Introduce a trace amount of zirconium that preferentially segregates to grain and phase boundaries by modifying the powder metallurgy process and a tailored low-temperature annealing step.
hypotheses.conditions: Test mechanical behavior at room temperature and slightly sub-ambient temperatures where segregation effects become critical under tensile loading.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enriched Zr segregation at the grain and phase boundaries which alters the local chemical composition and atomic bonding
hypotheses.mechanism: Zr atoms segregate at the boundaries, increasing the local interfacial energy and atomic order. This enhanced cohesion at the interface impedes the continuous dislocation transfer mechanism across FCC/BCC boundaries that is key in dissipating strain. As a result, dislocation pile-ups and reduced capacity for crack deflection/bridging promote premature strain localization and brittle failure—a departure from the ductile response observed in the untreated HEA.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The Zr-doped alloy will display lower fracture toughness and a reduction in work-hardening capacity (e.g., a sharper drop in strain-hardening rate) compared to the baseline HEA, with increased evidence of crack initiation at boundaries.
hypotheses.baseline: The original HEA with a balanced, enamel-like nanolamellar structure and stable dislocation transfer mechanisms, as reported in the paper.
hypotheses.boundary: Applicable under service conditions requiring a high strength–ductility balance at room to moderately low temperatures; effects may diminish at high temperatures where diffusion reduces segregation effects.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative change in toughness is uncertain due to possible compensating strengthening contributions from Zr-induced solid solution hardening.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two otherwise identical HEA samples—one with a controlled minor Zr addition and one without. Perform tensile and fracture toughness tests at room and low temperatures while characterizing grain-boundary compositions using TEM-EDS.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-doped sample does not show a statistically significant reduction in fracture toughness and exhibits similar dislocation transfer profiles as the baseline sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that phase boundaries mediate dislocation transfer in the HEA, as described in the paper.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes that intentional grain-boundary segregation (via Zr doping), while often used in conventional alloys to modify boundary cohesion, can disrupt the beneficial dislocation transfer mechanism in complex HEAs, leading to brittleness.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Brittle behavior emerges in the HEA at low temperatures due to suppressed dislocation nucleation and impaired phase-boundary mediated plasticity.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex HEA with alternating FCC and BCC lamellae that facilitates continuous dislocation migration as demonstrated in the paper.
hypotheses.intervention: Perform controlled tensile tests at cryogenic (e.g., -100 °C) versus room temperature and adjust the strain rate to investigate temperature-dependent dislocation activity.
hypotheses.conditions: Low testing temperatures and moderate strain rates where thermal activation for dislocation nucleation is limited.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The nanoscale phase boundaries between FCC and BCC phases which normally mediate dislocation transfer.
hypotheses.mechanism: At cryogenic temperatures, the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation and migration increases significantly. As a result, the phase-boundary mediated mechanism that relies on continuous dislocation transfer becomes inefficient. This leads to early strain localization, minimal plastic deformation, and preferential brittle crack propagation along or near the phase boundaries, in contrast to the ductile behavior at higher temperatures.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Under cryogenic testing, the HEA will exhibit a lower uniform elongation, a sharper decline in strain-hardening rate, and fracture surfaces with more cleavage features compared to the ductile baseline at room temperature.
hypotheses.baseline: The conventional performance of the HEA at room temperature, featuring strong work-hardening and energy dissipation via active dislocation transfer.
hypotheses.boundary: Valid for service conditions where the operating temperature drops near or below cryogenic levels; at intermediate temperatures, the effect may be less pronounced.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The magnitude of toughness degradation at cryogenic temperatures is uncertain due to potential contributions from alternative deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning) that might activate under extreme cooling.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct tensile tests on identical HEA samples at room temperature and at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., -100 °C) while mapping dislocation densities and tracking strain localization via in situ SEM or TEM.

hypotheses.hypothesis: In compositionally complex HEAs, deformation at low temperatures and high strain rates induces dislocation-mediated segregation of refractory elements (e.g. Ta and Mo) to grain boundaries, which lowers intergranular cohesion and promotes brittle fracture.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex HEA (e.g. MoNbTaTiV) with a homogeneous solid solution microstructure.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a controlled hot-deformation treatment at a relatively low temperature (within processing limits) combined with a high strain rate; compare with samples processed at higher temperatures and lower strain rates.
hypotheses.conditions: Deformation treatments performed at two regimes: one at lower temperature/high strain rate and the other at higher temperature/low strain rate; testing performed under conditions reflecting service stresses.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries enriched with segregated refractory elements.
hypotheses.mechanism: High strain rate and low temperature favor dislocation movement that drags high-melting-point elements (e.g. Ta, Mo) toward grain boundaries, causing localized segregation. This segregation reduces grain boundary cohesion, which ultimately decreases toughness and leads to brittle failure. In contrast, at higher temperatures and lower strain rates, enhanced diffusion promotes re-homogenization, preserving ductility.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples deformed at low temperature and high strain rate will show measurable reductions in fracture toughness (increased propensity for intergranular cracking) relative to those treated under higher temperature/low strain rate conditions. The magnitude of toughness loss is expected to be significant qualitatively, though precise numerical estimates are uncertain.
hypotheses.baseline: Single-phase HEA processed by hot deformation at conditions that do not promote significant segregation (i.e. higher temperature and lower strain rate) with ductile fracture characteristics.
hypotheses.boundary: The predicted brittle behavior is expected under service loading conditions where rapid deformation or sudden loadings occur at the relatively low temperature regime; outside these conditions, the effect may not be significant.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the trend is supported by observations of segregation in the paper (e.g. PMC11407990::web::004, PMC11407990::web::007), quantifying the exact degree of toughness reduction in the HEA remains uncertain.

hypotheses.hypothesis: In an initially single-phase HEA, cyclic thermal exposures (or thermal cycling) in service lead to localized diffusional fluxes at grain boundaries that produce thin, amorphous intergranular films enriched in specific solute elements, which in turn reduce grain boundary cohesion and trigger brittle behavior.

hypotheses.intervention: Expose the HEA to controlled thermal cycling under service-relevant temperatures (but below those causing complete phase transitions) to stimulate differential diffusional segregation, compared to isothermally annealed samples.
hypotheses.conditions: Thermal cycling with controlled heating and cooling rates (simulating service thermal fluctuations) versus constant temperature annealing; subsequent mechanical testing at ambient and elevated temperatures.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Development of thin, amorphous or compositionally distinct intergranular films along grain boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: Thermal cycling induces non-equilibrium diffusion processes at grain boundaries in the HEA. Local concentration gradients, accentuated by slight differences in atomic mobility among the constituent elements (especially those with lower melting points), can result in the formation of amorphous-like boundary films that lack the cohesive strength of the crystalline matrix. These continuous films act as weak interfaces, promoting brittle intergranular fracture during mechanical loading.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Thermally cycled samples would exhibit reduced fracture toughness and increased intergranular cracking compared to isothermally annealed specimens, with microstructural analyses (via high-resolution TEM) revealing the presence of amorphous or compositionally enriched films along the grain boundaries. The size of the toughness degradation is expected to be noticeable qualitatively, though quantification requires further investigation.

hypotheses.boundary: The effect is expected to be most pronounced under service conditions involving repeated thermal fluctuations, while steady-state thermal exposure may mitigate the development of amorphous films.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While diffusional segregation and amorphous intergranular film formation are known in other alloys (TXT::wikipedia::Segregation_(materials_science)::002), the quantitative impact on toughness in HEAs remains to be established.

Twin boundaries represent high-energy interfaces with crystallographic coherency different from typical grain boundaries. These interfaces can act as sinks for mobile solute atoms, leading to localized compositional perturbations. The resulting segregation may weaken the twin boundaries, turning them into preferential paths for crack initiation and propagation, thereby promoting brittle failure behavior.

hypotheses.uncertainty: Though deformation twinning and its association with local segregation have been observed in other materials, the exact influence on HEA toughness degradation and the quantitative differences between twinned and non-twinned conditions remain to be established.

paper_proposed: Proposed that controlled hot deformation conditions can be used as a tool to tailor grain boundary segregation and, by extension, the macroscopic properties of MoNbTaTiV refractory HEAs.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Intermediate-temperature embrittlement in single‐phase HEAs emerges from a strain-rate–dependent acceleration of dislocation‐enhanced nanoclustering of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) to grain boundaries. Lower strain rates allow more time for diffusion‐mediated nanoclustering during deformation, reducing GB cohesion and promoting brittle intergranular cracking.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A single-phase, coarse-grained CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with homogeneous elemental distribution and equiaxed grains (~50 μm).
hypotheses.intervention: Perform tensile tests at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 700°C) under two controlled strain-rate conditions (a standard strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 versus a higher strain rate).
hypotheses.conditions: Interrupted tensile deformation at intermediate temperatures, maintained in identical atmospheres and stress states; strain rates are the only variable.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Density and spatial distribution of nanoclusters at the grain boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: At lower strain rates, plastic deformation provides more time for dislocation-induced enhanced diffusion, facilitating the segregation and independent nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs. This leads to local reduction of GB cohesive energy and intergranular crack initiation, thereby degrading toughness. At higher strain rates, the kinetic window for segregation is narrower, reducing nanoclustering and preserving ductility.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The low strain-rate condition will show more extensive GB nanoclustering (observable via APT/TEM) and a transition toward brittle, intergranular fracture compared to the high strain-rate condition, which should exhibit more transgranular ductile failure.
hypotheses.baseline: Standard tensile tests at 700°C with 10^-3 s^-1 strain rate that already show ductility loss and GB cracking.
hypotheses.boundary: This effect is expected in the intermediate temperature range (400–800°C) and may not be significant at very low temperatures (where diffusion is limited) or very high temperatures (where nanoclusters may dissolve).
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in segregation extent and the threshold strain rates for switching behavior may require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical HEA samples and perform tensile tests at 700°C at two or more distinct strain rates. Use atom probe tomography (APT) and TEM to quantify the extent of GB nanoclustering. Correlate fracture modes (via SEM) and toughness measures with strain rate.
measurements: Grain boundary nanocluster density (APT, TEM)
Fracture surface morphology (SEM)
Engineering stress-strain response (tensile testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant difference in the extent of GB nanoclustering or fracture mode is observed between low and high strain rates, then the hypothesis that strain rate modulates dislocation-enhanced nanoclustering is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The finding in the paper that nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries correlates with ductility loss in HEAs.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis links the kinetics of dislocation-mediated diffusion to strain rate, proposing a controlled comparison that distinguishes kinetic segregation in HEAs from conventional impurity segregation mechanisms.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Brittle behavior in single-phase HEAs at intermediate temperature can be mitigated by tailoring the grain boundary character distribution (GBCD); specifically, increasing the fraction of low-energy (special) boundaries reduces the propensity for nanoclustering of principal elements and subsequent intergranular fracture.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A conventional, single-phase CrMnFeCoNi HEA with a random, high fraction of high-angle, high-energy grain boundaries (average grain size ~50 μm).
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a thermomechanical treatment (e.g., controlled sub-boundary annealing after cold rolling) designed to increase the proportion of low-energy, coherent or special grain boundaries (such as Σ3 twins).
hypotheses.conditions: Tensile testing at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 700°C) in identical atmospheres and deformation regimes, comparing treated versus untreated samples.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The nature and energy of grain boundaries that dictate the local diffusion and segregation behavior.
hypotheses.mechanism: Low-energy grain boundaries are less favorable sites for dislocation-enhanced nanoclustering, reducing the accumulation of embrittling Cr, Ni, and Mn clusters. This modification decreases the local reduction in cohesive energy and delays the onset of intergranular cracking, thus preserving toughness. In contrast, conventional random high-angle boundaries serve as rapid sinks for such nanoclusters.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples with an engineered high fraction of low-energy GBCD will exhibit less nanoclustering at GBs (observable with techniques such as APT) and will fracture in a more ductile, transgranular mode compared to untreated samples, which will show intergranular cracking and reduced ductility.
hypotheses.baseline: The untreated HEA state that shows marked ductility loss and intergranular cracking at intermediate temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: This approach is relevant for alloys that can sustain additional thermomechanical processing without compromising service properties. The beneficial effect is anticipated only if a significant fraction of low-energy boundaries is achieved.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The quantitative threshold for the beneficial fraction of special boundaries needed is uncertain, and grain boundary engineering may introduce other microstructural heterogeneities.

Degree of GB nanoclustering (APT, TEM)
Fracture mode and toughness (tensile testing, SEM)

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that nanoclustering-induced GB embrittlement drives ductility loss in HEAs.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a grain boundary engineering approach to modify the local chemical segregation behavior in HEAs, a method distinct from conventional impurity segregation control.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Enhancing grain boundary cohesion in single-phase HEAs by deliberate microalloying with elevated boron levels can counteract embrittlement. The hypothesis posits that sufficient boron segregation to grain boundaries will competitively inhibit the nanoclustering of embrittling Cr, Ni, and Mn, thereby mitigating intergranular cracking at intermediate temperatures.

hypotheses.intervention: Increase the boron content (e.g., to 0.2–0.5 at %) during alloy preparation while maintaining overall compositional complexity and single-phase stability.
hypotheses.conditions: Tensile testing at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 700°C) under identical deformation and environmental conditions for both B-enhanced and standard HEA samples.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at grain boundaries altering the local chemistry and energy landscape.
hypotheses.mechanism: At elevated concentrations, boron has a strong affinity for grain boundaries, where it can lower the GB energy and occupy sites that would otherwise accommodate nanoclusters of Cr, Ni, and Mn. This competitive segregation limits the formation of deleterious nanoclusters, preserves GB cohesion, and delays brittle fracture initiation compared to conventional HEAs. Unlike conventional alloys where impurity segregation is often inadvertent and deleterious, here boron is purposefully added to stabilize the GB structure.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The B-enhanced alloy will show a reduced extent of nanoclustering of the principal embrittling elements at GBs (detectable via APT/TEM), exhibit a more ductile (transgranular) fracture mode, and demonstrate improved toughness at 700°C relative to the standard alloy.
hypotheses.baseline: The standard CrMnFeCoNi HEA with minimal boron, which shows pronounced GB nanoclustering and brittle intergranular failure at intermediate temperatures.
hypotheses.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected if boron does not precipitate as brittle borides; thus, the upper limit of B addition must be below the threshold for secondary phase formation. The improvement is relevant primarily at intermediate to high temperatures where diffusion allows segregation.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal boron concentration is uncertain; too high a level may lead to the formation of brittle compounds, complicating interpretation.

paper_proposed: A GB segregation engineering strategy that migrates the fast segregation of embrittling principal elements from grain boundaries into preexisting Cr‐rich secondary phases.
That further optimization (in terms of morphology, dimension, and distribution) of these secondary phases may tailor the strength‐ductility‐temperature relations in HEAs.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Prolonged high-temperature exposure will induce subtle grain-boundary segregation in an initially single‐phase HEA, leading to nanoscale precipitation at the grain boundaries that degrades toughness via intergranular embrittlement.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase high-entropy alloy with a uniform BCC solid-solution structure.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject the alloy to long-duration annealing at a service-relevant elevated temperature (e.g., 900–1100 °C) below the melting point but over hundreds to thousands of hours.
hypotheses.conditions: Elevated temperature aging in an inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; comparison with as-homogenized baseline alloy.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Diffusional redistribution and segregation of certain constituent elements (e.g., Mo, Nb, Ta) to grain boundaries and subsequent nanoscale precipitation.
hypotheses.mechanism: At extended high temperatures, even in a well‐mixed HEA, the diffusivities of some elements lead to preferred segregation at grain boundaries. This may trigger the formation of fine, brittle precipitates (analogous to intergranular borides in conventional alloys) that reduce grain boundary cohesion. The mechanism contrasts with the conventional grain-boundary engineering in simpler alloys because the HEA’s high mixing entropy initially suppresses intermetallic formation; however, prolonged thermal exposure allows local compositional fluctuations overcoming this stabilization.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Aged samples will exhibit a transition from predominantly transgranular ductile fracture to a higher fraction of intergranular brittle fracture with reduced toughness, and the grain boundaries will show detectable nanometer-scale precipitates compared to the baseline.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-processed, single-phase HEA which demonstrates transgranular fracture with high work hardenability and ductility.
hypotheses.boundary: Service at elevated temperatures over long durations; loading under quasi-static conditions.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise segregation kinetics and precipitate size/distribution may vary; magnitude of toughness reduction is uncertain without detailed diffusion data.

paper_did: Prepared two variants of an equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA): one as‐cast and homogenized, and a second with a minor boron addition (0.1 at.%) via TiB2, using arc melting, triple remelting, homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 h, and water quenching.

Characterized the microstructure and chemical composition by XRD, SEM (with EDS), EBSD, and EPMA, observing that both alloys form a BCC solid‐solution matrix while the boron‐doped sample (RHEA-B) additionally shows intergranular precipitation of a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) (Hf, Zr)B2 phase and grain refinement (grain size reduced from ~130 μm to ~40 μm).

Evaluated mechanical properties using Vickers hardness tests, instrumented nanoindentations on different crystallographic orientations, in situ micropillar compression tests, and macro-compressive tests, documenting yield strengths, work hardenability, ductility, and fracture modes (a shift from intergranular fracture in RHEA to predominant transgranular fracture in RHEA-B).

The RHEA-B sample shows significant grain refinement, enhanced work hardenability, and improved ductility compared to the as‐cast RHEA, with a change in the failure mode from predominantly intergranular to primarily transgranular fracture.
A diminished anisotropy in elastic modulus and hardness across differently oriented grains was observed, attributed to the inherent lattice distortions in the high-entropy system.

This leads to premature crack initiation along weakened boundaries, contrasting with conventional grain-boundary precipitation damage.

paper_did: Synthesized an interstitial TWIP‐TRIP high‐entropy alloy (iHEA) with nominal composition Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 via vacuum induction melting, casting, hot‐rolling, homogenization, water‐quenching, and further cold‐rolling plus short-time annealing to refine the grain size.

paper_reported: Demonstrated that the addition of interstitial carbon increases stacking fault energy, thereby tuning the f.c.c. matrix phase’s instability to jointly activate nano‐twinning (TWIP) and transformation‐induced plasticity (TRIP) mechanisms.

Identified multiple strengthening contributions including substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening, the micro‐composite effect from a dual-phase structure, nano‐particle (M23C6 carbide) strengthening via Orowan mechanism, and conventional dislocation hardening and grain size reduction.

Showed that the optimized interstitial TWIP‐TRIP‐HEA achieves an exceptional combination of high strength and ductility with a marked improvement over single‐phase and previously developed TRIP‐DP systems.
paper_proposed: Proposed that interstitial alloying (with carbon) offers a new alloy design concept to tune phase (in)stability and activate an unprecedented combination of deformation and strengthening mechanisms within one material.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Low-temperature cyclic fatigue loading in the dual-phase iHEA promotes interphase decohesion at the f.c.c./h.c.p. interfaces, which leads to premature brittle-like failure under service conditions.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A dual-phase interstitial TWIP–TRIP HEA with an f.c.c. γ matrix, laminate h.c.p. ε phase, and homogeneously dispersed nano-carbides resulting from standard processing procedures.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject samples to controlled cyclic fatigue loading at a reduced temperature (e.g., around –50 °C) and compare the results with samples deformed under monotonic loading or cyclic loading at room temperature.
hypotheses.conditions: Fatigue tests should be conducted under low-temperature conditions where atomic mobility is reduced, so that any interfacial damage or decohesion between the f.c.c. and h.c.p. phases is more likely to be retained. Loading amplitudes should mimic extreme service conditions.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Decohesion and microcrack initiation along the interfaces between the f.c.c. matrix and the h.c.p. phase.
hypotheses.mechanism: Under cyclic fatigue at low temperatures, the differing mechanical responses of the f.c.c. and h.c.p. phases generate cyclic stresses concentrated at their interfaces. With reduced atomic mobility at low temperature, microdamage and microcracks accumulate along these interphase boundaries without efficient healing. Over multiple cycles, this leads to decohesion at the f.c.c./h.c.p. interfaces, providing preferential sites for brittle crack initiation and propagation.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to low-temperature cyclic fatigue loading will exhibit a lower fatigue life, reduced toughness, and fracture surfaces decorated with signs of interphase decohesion, in contrast to samples tested under room-temperature or monotonic loading conditions.
hypotheses.baseline: Dual-phase iHEA samples deformed under monotonic loading at room temperature, which show active TWIP/TRIP behavior with uniformly distributed deformation mechanisms and ductile fracture characteristics.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under cyclic loading at sufficiently low temperatures; at higher temperatures or under monotonic loading, the ductile mechanisms observed in the baseline will prevail.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact cyclic strain amplitude and frequency threshold required to trigger significant interphase decohesion in the dual-phase system is not fully determined.

hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated when the carbon content is increased moderately within the compositional complexity of the HEA; if carbon content is raised too high it could trigger other phase transformations that fall outside the intended design scope.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise threshold of carbon enrichment at which the beneficial TRIP/TWIP balance is upset, and the quantitative reduction in toughness, are not fully known.

paper_did: Synthesized a dual‐phase interstitial TWIP–TRIP high‐entropy alloy (iHEA) with nominal composition Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 via casting, hot‐rolling, homogenization, cold‐rolling, and rapid (short‐time) annealing.

Developed and compared two microstructural states – a coarse‐grained (homogenized) state with a ~160 μm grain size and a grain‐refined state (≈4.0 μm grain size) – that both exhibit a dual‐phase microstructure consisting of an f.c.c. γ matrix and a laminate h.c.p. ε phase, with uniformly distributed nano‐sized M23C6 carbides.
Characterized the alloy using XRD, EBSD, EDS, TEM, APT and conducted room‐temperature tensile tests to assess strength, ductility, strain‐hardening, and deformation mechanisms.
paper_reported: Demonstrated an exceptional strength–ductility combination: the iHEA achieved nearly twice the tensile strength of a single‐phase equiatomic alloy while maintaining ductility similar to benchmark dual‐phase HEAs.

Identified multiple concurrent strengthening and deformation mechanisms in the iHEA, including transformation‐induced plasticity (TRIP: f.c.c. to h.c.p. transformation), twinning‐induced plasticity (TWIP via nano‐twinning), stacking fault formation, dislocation hardening, and Orowan strengthening from nano‐carbides.

Showed that grain refinement leads to enhanced yield and ultimate strength (with a slight trade‐off in elongation) and that interstitial carbon plays a key role in tuning the stacking fault energy and phase stability of the alloy.
paper_proposed: Suggested that interstitial alloying (via carbon addition) provides an additional tuning parameter to optimize the balance between f.c.c. stability and transformation kinetics, offering further optimization potential in mechanical properties.

Implied that future work could explore processing modifications and compositional adjustments (e.g., via interstitial-driven phase tuning) to exploit the complete spectrum of metallic strengthening mechanisms in these HEAs.

hypotheses.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, a controlled slow cooling rate following casting enhances atomic mobility and promotes microsegregation of Ta and Zr toward grain boundaries. This leads to the formation of brittle intergranular precipitates that degrade toughness.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr HEA produced by vacuum arc melting.
hypotheses.intervention: Vary the cooling rate post-casting by comparing a rapid quench (to freeze the single-phase state) vs. a controlled slow cooling schedule.
hypotheses.conditions: Room temperature tensile tests on samples processed with both rapid quenching and slow cooling; identical casting and melting conditions otherwise.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Enhanced segregation and formation of Ta-rich precipitates at the grain boundaries.
hypotheses.mechanism: Slower cooling provides sufficient time for diffusion-driven atomic migration. Ta and Zr, which have a known tendency to segregate (as seen in the studied MEAs in PMC7514597::web::013 and PMC7514597::web::010), accumulate at grain boundaries and precipitate as brittle phases. This microstructural change reduces the content of the ductile BCC1 phase and weakens grain boundary cohesion, leading to lower elongation and toughness.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples will show reduced elongation to failure, increased intergranular fracture features, and a measurable decrease in BCC1 phase fraction compared to rapidly quenched samples. The change in toughness could be substantial (brittle behavior emerging with near-zero elongation in severe cases) relative to the baseline rapid-quench state.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-cast, rapidly quenched HEA with a predominantly single-phase BCC structure and high toughness.
hypotheses.boundary: Effect most pronounced at room temperature and under quasi-static tensile loading; results may vary if the alloy is later subjected to thermal aging.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in toughness is uncertain due to the complex interplay of diffusion kinetics and local composition variations.

Perform identical room temperature tensile tests and microstructural characterization (SEM, XRD, WDS) to measure the presence of intergranular precipitates and the fraction of the BCC1 phase.
measurements: Tensile elongation to failure
Fracture surface analysis
Phase quantification (BCC1 vs. secondary phases)

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If slow-cooled samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in ductility and no evidence of enhanced grain-boundary Ta/Zr-rich precipitates is observed compared to quenched samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper's finding that a higher combined Ta and Zr content correlates with reduced ductility through the formation of secondary BCC phases and grain-boundary precipitates.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It tests the role of cooling rate as a processing parameter that triggers the mechanistic transition from a ductile single-phase state to a brittle segregated microstructure, distinct from compositional changes.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount of a grain-boundary cohesion enhancer (such as boron) into a compositionally complex HEA suppresses the detrimental effects of Ta and Zr segregation, thereby retaining toughness even if local segregation tendencies exist.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous HfNbTaTiZr HEA with known sensitivity to Ta and Zr segregation.
hypotheses.intervention: Minor alloying addition of approximately 0.5 atomic percent boron during the melting process.
hypotheses.conditions: Casting under identical conditions with rapid cooling to preserve the single-phase state; subsequent room temperature tensile testing; comparative analysis between boron-doped and undoped alloys.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Boron atoms segregate to grain boundaries, increasing boundary cohesion and potentially interacting with segregating Ta and Zr to inhibit detrimental precipitate nucleation.
hypotheses.mechanism: Boron has been used in other alloy systems (e.g., superalloys) to improve grain-boundary cohesion and reduce embrittlement. By preferentially segregating to grain boundaries, boron may lower the energy of these interfaces and diminish the driving force for Ta/Zr precipitation as indicated by known segregation principles (TXT::wikipedia::Segregation_(materials_science)::002). This stabilizes the microstructure and maintains a higher fraction of the ductile BCC1 phase.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped HEA is expected to exhibit higher elongation to failure and a more ductile fracture morphology than the undoped baseline. Improvements in toughness are anticipated to be significant relative to the brittle behavior observed in Ta+Zr enriched compositions.
hypotheses.baseline: A rapidly quenched, undoped HfNbTaTiZr HEA that under identical conditions shows some level of grain-boundary segregation leading to reduced ductility.
hypotheses.boundary: Effectiveness may be limited to room temperature tensile behavior; the influence may differ under high-temperature service due to altered diffusion kinetics.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of toughness improvement is uncertain due to potential interactions of boron with other elements and the complexity of grain-boundary chemistry.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) followed by a short, controlled annealing treatment can homogenize the microstructure of a single-phase HEA by dissolving early-stage Ta and Zr segregation, thus preventing the evolution into brittle behavior.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An as-cast, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr HEA that is susceptible to minor segregation of Ta and Zr during solidification.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply SPD (e.g., high-pressure torsion) to refine the microstructure, followed by a short annealing treatment near the recovery temperature.
hypotheses.conditions: Processing carried out at room temperature with subsequent short annealing (e.g., 500 °C for 1 hour) to allow recovery without significant phase decomposition; mechanical testing at room temperature under quasi-static tensile loading.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain refinement and induced high dislocation densities promote re-dissolution of any incipient segregation, thus increasing the proportion of the ductile BCC1 phase and reducing intergranular precipitate formation.
hypotheses.mechanism: SPD introduces a high density of defects and refines the grain size, effectively enhancing atomic mixing and reducing segregation. The subsequent short anneal allows for partial recovery without permitting long-range diffusion that drives Ta and Zr segregation. As a result, the microstructure becomes more chemically homogeneous and retains superior toughness. This rationale is inspired by the understanding that deformation processing can modify segregation tendencies (as suggested by general plasticity principles and microstructural refinement strategies in TXT::doitpoms::mechanical_testing_metals/plasticity::001).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The SPD-treated and annealed HEA is expected to exhibit increased ductility (higher elongation to failure), a more uniform BCC1 phase distribution, and predominantly transgranular ductile fracture features compared to the untreated baseline.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-cast, rapidly quenched HEA which shows some degree of Ta and Zr segregation leading to partial brittle behavior under tensile load.
hypotheses.boundary: The treatment is expected to be effective for room temperature performance; its efficacy under high-temperature service might be diminished if thermally activated segregation occurs during prolonged exposure.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The extent of improved homogenization and its quantitative effect on toughness remains somewhat uncertain due to potential competing effects of work hardening and recovery during annealing.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s indication that minor segregation and phase decomposition (loss of the BCC1 phase) correlate with reduced toughness, combined with principles from deformation metallurgy regarding grain refinement and homogenization.

paper_did: Prepared a series of 3‐ and 4‐element medium entropy alloys (MEAs) derived from the HfNbTaTiZr system via vacuum arc melting with multiple remelts and no post‐casting heat treatment.

Conducted a range of room temperature mechanical tests (tensile testing, Vickers hardness) along with microstructural analyses using SEM, wavelength dispersive spectroscopy (WDS), and X‐ray diffraction (XRD) to characterize phase composition and segregation.

Performed an ab‐initio Monte Carlo simulation on the 5‐element HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy (HEA) to assess its equilibrium atomic configuration and reveal potential segregation (e.g., Ta “wires” in the structure).
paper_reported: The 5‐element HEA HfNbTaTiZr exhibits the best combination of strength and ductility compared to the 3‐ and 4‐element MEAs, which generally show lower strength and variable ductility.

A clear correlation was observed: increased Ta and Zr content leads to a decline in the ductile BCC1 phase, the formation of multiple BCC phases (BCC1, BCC2, and sometimes BCC3), and the development of brittle intergranular Ta‐rich precipitates.

Microstructural heterogeneities such as dendritic segregation and phase decomposition, as well as the metastable nature suggested by the Monte Carlo simulation, are linked to the observed variations in tensile properties (ductile vs. brittle behavior).
paper_proposed: Investigate the influence of cooling rate on phase composition and the extent of Ta/Zr segregation during solidification.
Perform further studies to elucidate the nature and formation mechanisms of secondary BCC phases (BCC2, BCC3) and intergranular precipitates.
Examine the stabilizing effect of Hf on HCP phase formation during mid‐temperature aging and explore long‐term aging/annealing behavior in related refractory alloys.

hypotheses.hypothesis: In a single‐phase high-entropy alloy, extremely high dislocation densities generated by SPD create enhanced diffusion paths, which during annealing trigger grain boundary segregation and chemical partitioning. This segregation leads to the formation of distinct boundary phases (e.g., a Nb/Ti‐rich bcc phase and a Hf/Zr‐rich bcc phase) along the grain boundaries. The resulting chemical inhomogeneity locally weakens the grain boundary cohesion and promotes intergranular fracture, thereby reducing toughness.

hypotheses.intervention: Prepare two sets of samples with identical overall composition but varying imposed shear strains during HPT (low strain at disk center vs. high strain at disk edge), followed by identical annealing treatments at a temperature (e.g., 740 K) where phase decomposition has been observed.

hypotheses.mechanism: High SPD-induced dislocation densities enhance atomic mobility along grain boundaries. The newly formed, chemically distinct phases at the boundaries have mismatched lattice parameters and moduli, weakening the cohesive strength of grain boundaries and promoting brittle (intergranular) cracking.

paper_did: Synthesized an equimolar HfNbTiZr multi‐principal element alloy (MPEA) via magnetic levitation melting, followed by a homogenization heat treatment.

Processed the alloy into disks and applied severe plastic deformation using high‐pressure torsion (HPT) with varying numbers of turns (½, 1, 5, and 10) and at two distinct locations (center with low shear strain and edge with high shear strain).
Subjected the HPT‐processed samples to annealing treatments at selected temperatures (740 K, 890 K, and 1000 K) with controlled heating and quenching rates.

Characterized the phase composition and microstructural evolution using X‐ray diffraction (including peak profile analysis), electron microscopy (SEM, TEM, EBSD), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and synchrotron XRD.
Measured mechanical response via Vickers microhardness tests.
paper_reported: Annealing at 740 K induced decomposition of the single bcc phase into two distinct bcc phases (bccL and bccH) with different lattice constants that are attributed to chemical partitioning (Hf/Zr‐rich vs. Nb/Ti‐rich compositions).
At higher annealing temperatures and in high-strain regions, an additional hcp phase emerged, with its fraction increasing (up to ~15% at 1000 K in high-strain areas).

Increased shear strain (from HPT) led to progressively refined crystallite sizes and higher dislocation densities, which then showed saturation after a threshold strain, and annealing at 740 K caused recovery (evidenced by increased crystallite size and reduced dislocation density in the bccH phase).

Hardness variations were observed; specifically, anneal-induced hardening occurred at 740 K for both low and high strain regions, while a softening was noted in high-strain samples between 740 K and 1000 K.
paper_proposed: Extended the previous study by investigating the influence of varying shear strain during HPT (via different turns and disk locations) on the thermal stability and phase evolution of the HfNbTiZr MPEA.
Implied that further work is needed to correlate the evolution of microstructural features (phase decomposition, recovery, dislocation density changes) with the resulting mechanical properties.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Enhanced grain‐boundary segregation of the Hf/Zr‐rich bccL phase in high-strain HEA regions promotes interfacial decohesion and brittle fracture.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase HfNbTiZr high-entropy alloy processed by HPT, with a homogeneous bcc structure and a uniform distribution of the four elements.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject separate batches of the HEA to different degrees of shear strain using HPT (e.g., selecting regions near the disk center for low strain and near the edge for high strain). Anneal all samples between 740 K and 890 K under identical conditions to induce bcc phase splitting. Use atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM coupled with EDS mapping specifically at and near grain boundaries to quantify the segregation of the Hf/Zr-enriched bccL phase.
hypotheses.conditions: Room-temperature mechanical fracture tests (micro-cantilever bending or notched specimens) performed at a fixed loading rate; annealing times and quenching rates kept constant to isolate the effects of strain-induced diffusion and segregation.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that become enriched in bccL phase owing to accelerated diffusion along high-angle boundaries in regions of high imposed strain.
hypotheses.mechanism: High shear strain increases the density of defects and grain-boundary area, which in turn accelerates grain-boundary diffusion during subsequent annealing. As the single-phase bcc matrix decomposes into bccL (enriched in larger Hf/Zr atoms) and bccH phases, the bccL phase preferentially diffuses and segregates to grain boundaries where diffusion pathways are more active. This localized enrichment reduces the interfacial cohesion (due to the lower bonding strength associated with the larger atomic radii), therefore predisposing these boundaries to intergranular brittle fracture under load.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: High-strain specimens will exhibit a measurable increase (qualitatively observed by APT/TEM-EDS) of Hf/Zr concentration at grain boundaries relative to low-strain specimens. Corresponding fracture tests will show lower fracture toughness and predominantly intergranular fracture modes in high-strain samples compared to the ductile behavior of specimens without significant grain-boundary enrichment.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-HPT processed HEA showing a homogeneous single-phase bcc structure with no preferential grain-boundary segregation and high toughness under comparable fracture tests.
hypotheses.boundary: Applies to HEA service conditions where the material is thermally exposed in the range of 740–890 K, without forming extensive intermetallic precipitates, and where deformation-induced strain heterogeneity exists.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact quantitative threshold of segregated Hf/Zr at the grain boundaries necessary for a significant drop in interfacial cohesion is not fully determined.

hypotheses.material_initial_state: An HfNbTiZr HEA processed by HPT exhibiting a high dislocation density and a nanocrystalline, single-phase bcc structure with relatively uniform initial residual stress distribution.
hypotheses.intervention: Subject the HEA to HPT processing followed by targeted annealing at temperatures (e.g., 740 K) that are high enough to trigger recovery but below the onset of extensive phase decomposition. hypotheses.conditions: Fracture tests (micro-cantilever or bending tests) performed at room temperature under identical loading rates; annealing must be controlled in time and temperature to emphasize recovery effects over new phase formation.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The differential recovery between grain interiors and boundaries, resulting in localized residual stress gradients.
hypotheses.mechanism: During annealing, the dislocation density in the high strain regions may be reduced non-uniformly, with grain boundaries—having faster recovery kinetics—achieving a lower dislocation density relative to the interior subgrains. Under subsequent mechanical loading, these residual stress gradients exaggerate the local stress intensity, facilitating crack initiation and brittle fracture, even though the overall microstructure remains single-phase.

hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be active for service conditions where the HEA experiences moderate thermal exposure that leads to recovery (around 740 K) without triggering significant phase decomposition.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of the residual stress gradients required to initiate brittle crack propagation is not well quantified in this system.

paper_did: Synthesized a homogeneous, equimolar refractory HfNbTiZr multi‐principal element alloy via magnetic levitation melting followed by homogenization heat treatment.

Processed the alloy by high‐pressure torsion (HPT) with various numbers of turns (½, 1, 5, and 10) to impose a wide range of shear strains (approximately 3 to 340) and sampled both disk centers and edges.
Annealed the HPT‐processed specimens at controlled temperatures (740, 890, and 1000 K) using constant heating (40 K/min) and quenching (300 K/min) conditions.

Conducted comprehensive microstructural characterization using X-ray diffraction (including phase identification by Lorentzian peak fitting), X-ray line-profile analysis for crystallite size and dislocation density, electron microscopy (EBSD, TEM, and EDS), and synchrotron XRD to assess through‐thickness homogeneity.

Measured mechanical properties via Vickers hardness testing and correlated the observed anneal-induced recovery and phase decomposition (splitting of the single bcc phase into bccL and bccH, and formation of an hcp phase at high strain) with processing conditions.
paper_reported: A single-phase bcc HfNbTiZr alloy decomposes into two distinct bcc phases (bccL and bccH) upon annealing at 740 K, with bccH dominating for most conditions.
At higher shear strains and/or higher annealing temperatures (above 890 K), an additional hcp phase appears, and the phase fractions vary with the imposed strain.
Annealing at 740 K leads to recovery in the bccH phase, evidenced by a significant reduction in dislocation density and an increase in the crystallite size relative to the as-HPT state.

Chemical heterogeneities develop upon annealing with differences in lattice parameters suggesting that the bccL phase is enriched in larger atoms (Hf/Zr) while the bccH phase is enriched in smaller atoms (Nb/Ti), and these changes correlate with variations in hardness.
paper_proposed: Extend the previous study by evaluating the influence of a wide range of HPT-induced shear strains (via different HPT turns and sampling positions) on annealing-induced microstructural evolution and phase decomposition.

Correlate the resulting phase compositions, microstructural parameters (such as crystallite size and dislocation density), and chemical heterogeneities with hardness variations, thereby shedding light on the thermal stability of the nanocrystalline HfNbTiZr MPEA.
